screens.title: What is a VLAN?
screens.narratorSegment: A Virtual Local Area Network, or VLAN, is a logical grouping of devices that share a broadcast domain even when connected to different physical switch ports. That means VLAN membership is defined by configuration, not by physical wiring. The practical benefit is that devices in one VLAN will not receive broadcast frames from another VLAN, which directly reduces unnecessary processing and keeps sensitive traffic isolated. Consider a small company with Sales, HR, and IT groups. Without VLANs, ARP requests and other broadcasts flood every device, potentially overwhelming user devices and creating security noise. By assigning Sales to VLAN 10, HR to VLAN 20, and IT to VLAN 30, each group stays isolated at Layer 2. Remember that VLANs are not routers. If you need devices in two VLANs to communicate, you need a Layer 3 device — a router or a Layer 3 switch — to perform inter-VLAN routing. A common misconception is thinking VLANs provide encryption or full security by themselves; VLANs separate broadcast domains and help enforce policy, but additional controls like ACLs or firewalls are required for robust isolation. For practice, imagine moving a laptop from one switch port to another: if both ports are in VLAN 10, the laptop remains in the same broadcast domain without any change to its IP configuration. Ask yourself: how would this behavior change if inter-VLAN routing were configured on a router?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A VLAN is a logical broadcast domain configured on switches that isolates broadcasts and groups devices logically.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is a VLAN?
VLAN definition

A VLAN groups devices into a single logical broadcast domain regardless of physical port locations.

Analogy
Think of VLANs as separate rooms in a building: people in one room can talk freely while people in other rooms do not hear those conversations.
Concrete example
Sales devices are placed in VLAN 10, HR in VLAN 20, IT in VLAN 30. Broadcasts from Sales do not reach HR or IT without routing.
Common misconception
VLANs do not encrypt traffic. They only isolate broadcast domains; use ACLs or firewalls for stronger security.
Key Takeaway

VLANs logically separate broadcast traffic so you can group users by role or function without rewiring switches.

Behavior example
Scenario
A PC on GigabitEthernet0/1 is assigned VLAN 10. When it broadcasts an ARP request, only ports in VLAN 10 receive it. Moving the PC to another port assigned to VLAN 10 does not change its broadcast domain.
Why it matters
Reduced broadcast traffic improves performance on endpoints and switches, and segmentation helps contain issues within a department.

screens.title: Creating VLANs on a Cisco Switch
screens.narratorSegment: Creating VLANs on a Cisco switch is a simple two-step process: define the VLAN globally and then assign ports to it. First, you enter global configuration mode and use the vlan command with the VLAN ID, then optionally give it a descriptive name. This makes show outputs readable and helps operations teams identify VLAN purpose quickly. Second, you navigate to the interface intended for an end device, set the port to access mode with switchport mode access, and then assign the access VLAN with switchport access vlan. A typical mistake is assigning a port to a VLAN that doesn't exist yet; the port will not behave as expected. Always create the VLAN before assigning ports, and verify with show vlan brief to confirm name and member ports. For an example, create VLAN 10 and name it Sales, then set GigabitEthernet0/1 as an access port in VLAN 10. After configuration, use show vlan brief to confirm VLAN 10 exists and shows Gi0/1 as a member. This practice ensures your VLAN inventory stays synchronized and reduces misconfiguration during troubleshooting. Creating VLANs on a Cisco Switch means always create vlans globally before assigning them to access ports; use descriptive names and verify with show vlan brief.. In practical terms, commands to create vlans and name them for clear inventory. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Creating VLANs
Create VLANs (high-level)
Define the VLAN ID, add a name for clarity, then assign ports to that VLAN as access ports.
Steps
  1. Create VLAN globally with vlan <id> and name.
  2. Go to interface and set switchport mode access.
  3. Set switchport access vlan <id> and add a description.
  4. Verify with show vlan brief.
Tip
Give VLANs meaningful names to reduce human error during troubleshooting.
Key Takeaway

Create VLANs before assignment, name them, and verify with show commands to avoid configuration gaps.

CLI Example
configure terminal
vlan 10
 name SALES
 exit
vlan 20
 name HR
 exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 description Connected to Sales PC
 exit
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 20
 description Connected to HR PC
 exit
Verify
Use show vlan brief to confirm VLAN names and member ports. If a port does not appear, check that the VLAN was created first.

screens.title: Access Ports: Assigning End Devices to VLANs
screens.narratorSegment: An access port is a switchport configured to carry traffic for only a single VLAN, typically used to connect end devices such as PCs, printers, or phones. The endpoint itself is unaware of VLAN tagging; the switch associates frames received on that port with the configured VLAN. This makes access ports straightforward to manage: configure the port mode to access and set the access VLAN. For example, setting GigabitEthernet0/1 to switchport mode access and switchport access vlan 10 ensures any host on that port is treated as a member of VLAN 10. A common operational step is adding a description so future operators understand the device connected to the port. Misconfigurations to watch for include leaving a port in trunk mode accidentally or assigning the wrong VLAN ID. In both cases, the endpoint will not join the intended broadcast domain. After configuring an access port, verify the setting using show interfaces interface switchport, which displays the administrative and operational mode and the access VLAN. This verification step helps you catch wrong port modes before they impact users. Access Ports: Assigning End Devices to VLANs means access ports map an untagged endpoint to a single vlan; set switchport mode access and switchport access vlan, then verify with show interfaces switchport.. In practical terms, how access ports behave and sample configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Access ports map an untagged endpoint to a single VLAN; set switchport mode access and switchport access vlan, then verify with show interfaces switchport.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Access Ports
Access port concept
An access port carries traffic for a single VLAN and presents untagged frames to the endpoint.
Behavior
Frames received untagged on the access port are associated with that interface's access VLAN and forwarded only to ports in the same VLAN.
Common mistake
Leaving a port set to trunk mode by mistake will prevent an attached PC from joining the intended VLAN.
Key Takeaway

Access ports simplify endpoint connectivity; always verify the port mode and access VLAN after configuration.

CLI Example
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 description Connected to Sales PC
 exit

! Verify the interface mode and VLAN assignment
show interfaces GigabitEthernet0/1 switchport
Verification
show interfaces interface switchport displays administrative and operational mode, the access VLAN, and trunking details if any. Use it to confirm your expected state.

screens.title: What is a Trunk Link and 802.1Q Tagging?
screens.narratorSegment: A trunk link connects two switches or a switch and router and carries traffic for multiple VLANs over a single physical connection. The mechanism that makes this possible is IEEE 802.1Q tagging. When a frame belonging to a VLAN traverses a trunk, 802.1Q inserts a four-byte tag into the Ethernet header that contains the VLAN ID. The receiving switch inspects the tag and forwards the frame to ports that are members of that VLAN. By default, trunks allow all VLANs, but you can restrict the list of VLANs that are permitted to reduce unnecessary traffic. There is also a concept called the native VLAN: frames belonging to that VLAN are sent untagged across the trunk. By default the native VLAN is VLAN 1, and mismatches in the native VLAN between two ends create subtle connectivity problems and console warnings. A misconception is thinking trunks authenticate or encrypt VLANs; trunks simply tag VLANs to transport them. Correct trunk setup and matching encapsulation on both ends are essential for predictable multi-switch VLAN connectivity. What is a Trunk Link and 802.1Q Tagging? means trunks carry multiple vlans by adding an 802.1q tag with the vlan id; native vlan traffic is untagged and must match on both ends.. In practical terms, carry multiple vlans over one link by tagging frames with a vlan id. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Trunks carry multiple VLANs by adding an 802.1Q tag with the VLAN ID; native VLAN traffic is untagged and must match on both ends.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Trunk & 802.1Q
Trunk concept
A trunk carries multiple VLANs; 802.1Q tags frames with a VLAN ID so the receiver can sort traffic correctly.
802.1Q tag
A 4-byte field inserted into the Ethernet header contains the VLAN ID used by the receiving switch to map frames to the correct VLAN.
Native VLAN
Traffic for the native VLAN is sent untagged. Native VLAN mismatches lead to connectivity issues for untagged traffic and console warnings.
Key Takeaway

802.1Q tagging allows many VLANs to share one link while preserving VLAN membership across switches.

Concrete example
Scenario
Switch1 sends a VLAN 10 frame across a trunk. The frame is tagged with VLAN 10. Switch2 receives the frame, reads the 802.1Q tag, and forwards it only to VLAN 10 ports. Frames in the native VLAN travel untagged and must match on both ends.
Misconception check
Tags do not encrypt or authenticate VLANs; they only identify VLAN membership. Use security controls for stronger isolation.

screens.title: Configuring a Trunk Port on Cisco IOS
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring a trunk port on a Cisco switch requires entering interface configuration and setting the port to trunk mode. Optionally you can specify encapsulation to dot1q; on many modern switches dot1q is the default, but explicitly setting encapsulation avoids ambiguity. You typically use switchport mode trunk and switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q, then define switchport trunk allowed vlan to restrict which VLANs traverse the trunk. For example, configuring GigabitEthernet0/24 as the uplink between switches would include switchport mode trunk, switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q, and switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,30 to limit traffic. Remember to add a description so administrators understand the link purpose. Also ensure the other end of the trunk uses the same encapsulation and allowed VLANs and that the native VLAN matches if you change it from the default. After configuration, verify the trunk with show interfaces trunk to see which VLANs are active and which ports are trunks. Proper trunk setup prevents VLAN leakage and ensures VLANs propagate as expected across your switching fabric. Configuring a Trunk Port on Cisco IOS means set switchport mode trunk, match encapsulation to 802.1q on both ends, and optionally restrict allowed vlans for cleaner traffic separation.. In practical terms, commands to set encapsulation, trunk mode, and allowed vlans. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Configuring Trunk Ports
Trunk commands
Set trunk mode, optionally set encapsulation, and restrict allowed VLANs if required by policy.
configure terminal
interface GigabitEthernet0/24  # uplink to Switch2
 switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20
 description Uplink to Switch2
 exit
Verify with show interfaces trunk to inspect active trunks and allowed VLANs. If VLANs do not appear, check allowed lists on both ends.
Pro Tip

Restricting allowed VLANs on trunks reduces unnecessary broadcast and improves control over what VLANs cross the link.

Check both ends
Match encapsulation
If one end is not set to 802.1Q, or uses a different encapsulation, the trunk won't carry VLAN traffic as expected.
Native VLAN
If you change the native VLAN from VLAN 1, ensure the change matches on the remote switch to avoid native VLAN mismatch issues.

screens.title: Access Port vs Trunk Port
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the difference between access and trunk ports is essential to correct VLAN deployment. An access port connects a single end device and carries traffic only for its configured VLAN; frames are untagged to the endpoint. Use access ports for user devices, printers, and phones. A trunk port connects switches or a switch to a router and carries traffic for multiple VLANs; frames are tagged with 802.1Q except for the native VLAN which travels untagged. Use trunk ports for uplinks between switches or to carry multiple VLANs to a router. A frequent mistake is configuring an uplink as an access port or accidentally leaving an end-user port in trunk mode; either misconfiguration prevents traffic from reaching the intended VLAN. When designing, choose access ports for endpoints and trunks for links that must carry more than one VLAN. Always verify with the right show commands: show interfaces interface switchport for port details, and show interfaces trunk for trunk summaries. As a quick check, ask: does this link need to carry more than one VLAN? If yes, make it a trunk; if no, keep it an access port.

narration.text: Understanding the difference between access and trunk ports is essential to correct VLAN deployment. An access port connects a single end device and carries traffic only for its configured VLAN; frames are untagged to the endpoint. Use access ports for user devices, printers, and phones. A trunk port connects switches or a switch to a router and carries traffic for multiple VLANs; frames are tagged with 802.1Q except for the native VLAN which travels untagged. Use trunk ports for uplinks between switches or to carry multiple VLANs to a router. A frequent mistake is configuring an uplink as an access port or accidentally leaving an end-user port in trunk mode; either misconfiguration prevents traffic from reaching the intended VLAN. When designing, choose access ports for endpoints and trunks for links that must carry more than one VLAN. Always verify with the right show commands: show interfaces interface switchport for port details, and show interfaces trunk for trunk summaries. As a quick check, ask: does this link need to carry more than one VLAN? If yes, make it a trunk; if no, keep it an access port.

screens.title: Native VLAN and Security Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: The native VLAN is the VLAN whose frames travel untagged across an 802.1Q trunk. By default that VLAN is VLAN 1. Leaving critical systems or management interfaces on VLAN 1 is a security risk because VLAN 1 is a well-known default and often receives unnecessary traffic. Best practice is to move management traffic to a dedicated, non-default VLAN and to change the native VLAN on trunks to an unused VLAN if you must use an untagged native. When you change the native VLAN, make sure both ends of the trunk share the same native VLAN to avoid native VLAN mismatch. A mismatch can cause untagged traffic to be misinterpreted and generate error messages on the switches. In practice, choose a specific VLAN ID for management, update the native VLAN consistently across trunks, and document the change in network diagrams. Remember that VLAN changes can impact device reachability, so schedule them during maintenance windows and verify reachability after changes using ping and show commands. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Common VLAN and Trunking Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: In practice, a small set of repeatable mistakes cause most VLAN and trunking outages. First, native VLAN mismatch occurs when each end of a trunk uses a different native VLAN; untagged frames are misinterpreted and console logs often show a mismatch error. Second, an allowed VLAN mismatch happens when one side permits a VLAN on the trunk and the other denies it; VLAN traffic will be dropped. Third, incorrect port mode — configuring an uplink as access or an access port as trunk — prevents devices from joining the proper VLAN. Fourth, forgetting to create a VLAN globally before assigning ports leaves ports in an undefined state. Troubleshooting follows a simple flow: check show interfaces trunk for trunk state and native VLAN, check show vlan brief for VLAN existence and member ports, and use show interfaces interface switchport to confirm interface mode and access VLAN. When you encounter an error, compare configuration on both ends of a trunk and correct mismatched native or allowed VLAN lists. Log your changes and re-verify to ensure the network returns to the expected state.

fullNarratorScript:
Today we’ll build an intuitive, practical view of VLANs and trunking so you can segment networks safely and carry many VLANs across a single link. You will learn what a VLAN is, why splitting a physical switch into multiple logical broadcast domains improves performance and security, and how to configure access ports to place devices into the correct VLAN. Next, we will examine trunk links and the IEEE 802.1Q tagging standard that lets multiple VLANs share one physical connection between switches. We’ll walk through the key Cisco IOS commands for creating VLANs, assigning access ports, and making a trunk with allowed VLAN lists. Along the way I’ll show common mistakes you will see in the field — for example, forgetting to create a VLAN before assigning it, mismatched native VLANs, or setting the wrong port mode — and how to verify and fix them using show commands. By the end of this lesson you will be able to plan a simple VLAN layout for departments, configure both access and trunk ports on Cisco switches, and use verification commands to diagnose basic trunking errors. Think about a small office with Students and Faculty VLANs: by the end you’ll be able to make those VLANs reach across two switches while keeping broadcasts isolated.

These learning objectives guide what you will practice and check during the lab. First, you will be able to explain the purpose and benefits of VLANs: how they create separate logical broadcast domains to improve security and reduce unnecessary broadcast traffic. Second, you'll learn to configure access ports on Cisco switches so end devices sit in the correct VLAN; this includes creating a VLAN and assigning it to a physical port. Third, you'll understand trunk links and the IEEE 802.1Q tag that identifies VLAN ID information as frames traverse a trunk between switches. Fourth, you'll configure trunk ports to carry multiple VLANs and optionally restrict which VLANs are allowed. Each of these objectives is practical — you will see commands, verify state with show commands, and test common troubleshooting steps. Together they give you both conceptual grounding and CLI practice, so you can deploy VLANs, interconnect switches, and diagnose basic trunking errors in a small campus network.

These objectives emphasize hands-on skills and safe configuration. First, you’ll practice creating VLANs globally and giving them descriptive names so your network documentation is clear. Second, you’ll assign access ports to VLANs and use show commands to verify the assignment; this validates device membership and helps you spot missing VLANs. Third, you’ll configure trunk ports between switches, including setting encapsulation to 802.1Q and optionally restricting allowed VLANs to reduce accidental traffic. Fourth, you will learn to identify and resolve common mistakes: native VLAN mismatch, allowed VLAN mismatch, incorrect port mode, and forgetting to create a VLAN before assigning it. Each objective will include a verification step using show vlan brief, show interfaces trunk, and show interfaces interface switchport. Practicing these steps gives you the muscle memory to avoid outages and to diagnose trunking problems quickly in a real network.

A Virtual Local Area Network, or VLAN, is a logical grouping of devices that share a broadcast domain even when connected to different physical switch ports. That means VLAN membership is defined by configuration, not by physical wiring. The practical benefit is that devices in one VLAN will not receive broadcast frames from another VLAN, which directly reduces unnecessary processing and keeps sensitive traffic isolated. Consider a small company with Sales, HR, and IT groups. Without VLANs, ARP requests and other broadcasts flood every device, potentially overwhelming user devices and creating security noise. By assigning Sales to VLAN 10, HR to VLAN 20, and IT to VLAN 30, each group stays isolated at Layer 2. Remember that VLANs are not routers. If you need devices in two VLANs to communicate, you need a Layer 3 device — a router or a Layer 3 switch — to perform inter-VLAN routing. A common misconception is thinking VLANs provide encryption or full security by themselves; VLANs separate broadcast domains and help enforce policy, but additional controls like ACLs or firewalls are required for robust isolation. For practice, imagine moving a laptop from one switch port to another: if both ports are in VLAN 10, the laptop remains in the same broadcast domain without any change to its IP configuration. Ask yourself: how would this behavior change if inter-VLAN routing were configured on a router?

Creating VLANs on a Cisco switch is a simple two-step process: define the VLAN globally and then assign ports to it. First, you enter global configuration mode and use the vlan command with the VLAN ID, then optionally give it a descriptive name. This makes show outputs readable and helps operations teams identify VLAN purpose quickly. Second, you navigate to the interface intended for an end device, set the port to access mode with switchport mode access, and then assign the access VLAN with switchport access vlan. A typical mistake is assigning a port to a VLAN that doesn't exist yet; the port will not behave as expected. Always create the VLAN before assigning ports, and verify with show vlan brief to confirm name and member ports. For an example, create VLAN 10 and name it Sales, then set GigabitEthernet0/1 as an access port in VLAN 10. After configuration, use show vlan brief to confirm VLAN 10 exists and shows Gi0/1 as a member. This practice ensures your VLAN inventory stays synchronized and reduces misconfiguration during troubleshooting. Creating VLANs on a Cisco Switch means always create vlans globally before assigning them to access ports; use descriptive names and verify with show vlan brief.. In practical terms, commands to create vlans and name them for clear inventory. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

An access port is a switchport configured to carry traffic for only a single VLAN, typically used to connect end devices such as PCs, printers, or phones. The endpoint itself is unaware of VLAN tagging; the switch associates frames received on that port with the configured VLAN. This makes access ports straightforward to manage: configure the port mode to access and set the access VLAN. For example, setting GigabitEthernet0/1 to switchport mode access and switchport access vlan 10 ensures any host on that port is treated as a member of VLAN 10. A common operational step is adding a description so future operators understand the device connected to the port. Misconfigurations to watch for include leaving a port in trunk mode accidentally or assigning the wrong VLAN ID. In both cases, the endpoint will not join the intended broadcast domain. After configuring an access port, verify the setting using show interfaces interface switchport, which displays the administrative and operational mode and the access VLAN. This verification step helps you catch wrong port modes before they impact users. Access Ports: Assigning End Devices to VLANs means access ports map an untagged endpoint to a single vlan; set switchport mode access and switchport access vlan, then verify with show interfaces switchport.. In practical terms, how access ports behave and sample configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A trunk link connects two switches or a switch and router and carries traffic for multiple VLANs over a single physical connection. The mechanism that makes this possible is IEEE 802.1Q tagging. When a frame belonging to a VLAN traverses a trunk, 802.1Q inserts a four-byte tag into the Ethernet header that contains the VLAN ID. The receiving switch inspects the tag and forwards the frame to ports that are members of that VLAN. By default, trunks allow all VLANs, but you can restrict the list of VLANs that are permitted to reduce unnecessary traffic. There is also a concept called the native VLAN: frames belonging to that VLAN are sent untagged across the trunk. By default the native VLAN is VLAN 1, and mismatches in the native VLAN between two ends create subtle connectivity problems and console warnings. A misconception is thinking trunks authenticate or encrypt VLANs; trunks simply tag VLANs to transport them. Correct trunk setup and matching encapsulation on both ends are essential for predictable multi-switch VLAN connectivity. What is a Trunk Link and 802.1Q Tagging? means trunks carry multiple vlans by adding an 802.1q tag with the vlan id; native vlan traffic is untagged and must match on both ends.. Configuring a trunk port on a Cisco switch requires entering interface configuration and setting the port to trunk mode. Optionally you can specify encapsulation to dot1q; on many modern switches dot1q is the default, but explicitly setting encapsulation avoids ambiguity. Understanding the difference between access and trunk ports is essential to correct VLAN deployment. An access port connects a single end device and carries traffic only for its configured VLAN; frames are untagged to the endpoint. Use access ports for user devices, printers, and phones. A trunk port connects switches or a switch to a router and carries traffic for multiple VLANs; frames are tagged with 802.1Q except for the native VLAN which travels untagged. Use trunk ports for uplinks between switches or to carry multiple VLANs to a router. A frequent mistake is configuring an uplink as an access port or accidentally leaving an end-user port in trunk mode; either misconfiguration prevents traffic from reaching the intended VLAN. When designing, choose access ports for endpoints and trunks for links that must carry more than one VLAN. Always verify with the right show commands: show interfaces interface switchport for port details, and show interfaces trunk for trunk summaries. As a quick check, ask: does this link need to carry more than one VLAN? If yes, make it a trunk; if no, keep it an access port.

The native VLAN is the VLAN whose frames travel untagged across an 802.1Q trunk. By default that VLAN is VLAN 1. Leaving critical systems or management interfaces on VLAN 1 is a security risk because VLAN 1 is a well-known default and often receives unnecessary traffic. Best practice is to move management traffic to a dedicated, non-default VLAN and to change the native VLAN on trunks to an unused VLAN if you must use an untagged native. When you change the native VLAN, make sure both ends of the trunk share the same native VLAN to avoid native VLAN mismatch. A mismatch can cause untagged traffic to be misinterpreted and generate error messages on the switches. In practice, choose a specific VLAN ID for management, update the native VLAN consistently across trunks, and document the change in network diagrams. Remember that VLAN changes can impact device reachability, so schedule them during maintenance windows and verify reachability after changes using ping and show commands. In practice, a small set of repeatable mistakes cause most VLAN and trunking outages. First, native VLAN mismatch occurs when each end of a trunk uses a different native VLAN; untagged frames are misinterpreted and console logs often show a mismatch error. Second, an allowed VLAN mismatch happens when one side permits a VLAN on the trunk and the other denies it; VLAN traffic will be dropped. Third, incorrect port mode — configuring an uplink as access or an access port as trunk — prevents devices from joining the proper VLAN. Fourth, forgetting to create a VLAN globally before assigning ports leaves ports in an undefined state. Troubleshooting follows a simple flow: check show interfaces trunk for trunk state and native VLAN, check show vlan brief for VLAN existence and member ports, and use show interfaces interface switchport to confirm interface mode and access VLAN. When you encounter an error, compare configuration on both ends of a trunk and correct mismatched native or allowed VLAN lists. Log your changes and re-verify to ensure the network returns to the expected state.

Summarizing the chapter helps cement the essentials. First, VLANs separate broadcast domains and let you group devices logically for improved performance and control. Second, access ports place a single endpoint into a single VLAN and are untagged to that device. Third, trunk ports carry many VLANs across a single physical link using IEEE 802.1Q tagging, and the native VLAN travels untagged. Fourth, always create VLANs before assigning them to ports, and name VLANs for clarity. Fifth, verification commands such as show vlan brief, show interfaces trunk, and show interfaces interface switchport are your primary tools for confirming correct operation. Sixth, common errors like native VLAN mismatches or allowed VLAN mismatches are easy to find with the right show outputs and are usually fixed by aligning configurations on both ends. Keep these points in mind as quick checks while you configure and troubleshoot VLANs and trunks.

Third, use the verification trio of show vlan brief, show interfaces trunk, and show interfaces interface switchport after every change.
